Fundamentals, explained

What Is Earnings Growth?

Whether a company's profits are growing — not just revenue, but the money it actually keeps.

So what is it, exactly?

Picture this: your paycheck went up 10% this year — but after rent, groceries, and gas, the amount actually landing in savings went down. Which number tells the real story? The one you keep. Companies work the same way. Revenue is the paycheck; earnings are what's left after every bill is paid. Earnings growth asks whether that leftover number is getting bigger each year.

Earnings — also called net income or the bottom line — are the profits that belong to shareholders. Earnings growth compares this year's profit to last year's. Growing earnings mean the business isn't just selling more; it's keeping more.

Why should you care?

Because over the long run, a stock's price tends to follow its earnings. A company that grows profits year after year is building real value you can measure — and eventually, the market notices. Revenue growth gets the headlines; earnings growth pays the bills.

It's also the perfect partner to the revenue check. Revenue up and earnings up? The business is scaling beautifully. Revenue up but earnings down? Growth is getting expensive — the company is buying its sales. That gap is one of the most useful warning signs in investing.

The grading scale
StrongEarnings growth above 10% — profits are accelerating
SolidEarnings growth of 3–10% — steady profit improvement
WeakEarnings growth below 3% or declining — profits under pressure

Let's make it real

Imagine two companies that each earned $2.00 per share last year. This year, Company A earns $2.30 per share. Company B earns $1.90. Same starting point — opposite directions.

Company A $2.30 EPS vs $2.00 last year
+15%
Profits are growing — each share earned more this year.
Company B $1.90 EPS vs $2.00 last year
−5%
Profits are shrinking — each share earned less.

One year doesn't make a trend — even great companies have down years. But a pattern of growing earnings is the closest thing investing has to a tailwind. Company A has it. Company B needs to explain where the profits went.
